name: Maya Yoshida
status: Free agent. His LA Galaxy contract ended on 20 Nov 2026. He has NOT announced retirement. Next step: undecided.
summary: Japanese centre-back (a defender who plays in the middle of the back line). He played in the top division of six countries, captained Japan at a World Cup, and captained LA Galaxy to the 2024 MLS Cup.
quick_facts: 2007 to 2026: Japan, Netherlands, England, Italy, Germany, USA
580 matches, 36 goals (all competitions, added up from the season table below)
Waseda University, School of Human Sciences (correspondence course), graduated 2019
President of the Japan Pro-Footballers Association (players' union) since 2022
seasons_note: Matches in all competitions (league, cups, continental). Source: English Wikipedia career table for 2007 to 2025; LA Galaxy official totals (117 matches, 8 goals) for the club total; 2026 is from Soccer King (28 matches, 2 goals), which matches the club total. Other sites count 2026 differently (see 'Not verified').

timeline.event: Born in Nagasaki, the youngest of three brothers.
Passes the Nagoya Grampus youth trial on a family trip, expecting to fail. Leaves home and moves to Aichi with an older brother.
Chooses a public high school (Toyota High School) partly to study English seriously, already aiming to play abroad.
Turns professional with Nagoya Grampus. Starts a Waseda University correspondence degree.
Plays at the Beijing Olympics (U-23). Wins a regular centre-back place at Nagoya under coach Dragan Stojković.
Best season in Japan: 48 matches, 8 goals. Signs for VVV-Venlo in December.
Senior Japan debut (6 Jan). Breaks a foot bone days after arriving in the Netherlands and misses about 10 months. Dutch league debut on 30 Oct.
Wins the AFC Asian Cup with Japan (first Japan goal, also a red card in the quarter-final). Scores against PSV in September.

Captains Japan to 4th place at the London Olympics. Joins Southampton (Premier League) for about £3 million on 30 Aug. 💍 Announces his marriage on his blog on 26 Sep (age 24), to a woman he had dated since his Nagoya days. She is not a public figure.
First full Premier League season: 34 matches. Criticised in Japan after the Confederations Cup.
First World Cup (Brazil): starts all 3 matches. At Southampton he is back-up behind Lovren and Fonte.
New 3-year Southampton contract (Jan). A back-pass mistake against Manchester United (Sept) sends him back to the bench.
Still third-choice at Southampton; uses cup games to stay ready. 👶 First child, a daughter, born at the end of November; he announces it on 16 Dec (age 28).

Breakthrough year: captains Southampton for the first time (18 Jan), plays the League Cup final at Wembley (26 Feb), first match as Japan captain (23 Mar), first Japanese player to reach 100 Premier League matches (29 Apr), new contract to 2020.
World Cup in Russia: plays every minute; Japan lose 3–2 to Belgium after leading 2–0. Becomes permanent Japan captain after Makoto Hasebe. Publishes his book 'Unbeatable Mind'.

Asian Cup runner-up as captain (his handball gives away a penalty in the final). Gets UK permanent residency. Graduates from Waseda. Pledges 1% of his wages to the Saints Foundation charity. 100th cap for Japan (14 Nov).
Moves to Sampdoria (Italy) on loan on deadline day (31 Jan). Debuts 8 Mar, right before lockdown. Donates 10,000 masks in Genoa. Gives a club interview in Italian by August.
Captains Japan to 4th at the Tokyo Olympics (his third Games). Scores against Inter Milan (12 Sept). Becomes Japan's most-capped centre-back (Nov).
Becomes president of the players' union (20 June). Joins Schalke 04 (5 July). Captains Japan at the Qatar World Cup: wins over Germany and Spain; loses to Croatia on penalties (his kick is saved).
Schalke are relegated (dropped to the second division). Joins LA Galaxy on 3 Aug. Left out of the Japan squad as a new generation takes over.
Captain of LA Galaxy. Starts every league match. Wins the MLS Cup (7 Dec), his first club trophy. Club Defender of the Year.
Signs a new 2-year deal (18 Jan) with a pay cut. Galaxy have a very bad season (14th in the West). 👶 Announces his second child, a son, on 12 Nov (age 37).

Farewell match for Japan (31 May, 127th cap). Travels to the World Cup as a non-playing support member. Gets a US green card (16 July). Loses his starting place from September; knee injury. Contract ends 20 Nov; future undecided.

achievements.item: MLS Cup winner (as captain), LA Galaxy
Three World Cups (11 matches); captain in 2022; round of 16 in 2018 and 2022
Three Olympics; captain twice; 4th place twice
127 caps for Japan: most ever by a Japanese centre-back; reported as 3rd on Japan's all-time list
First Japanese player to reach 100 Premier League matches; 154 in total is still the most by a Japanese player
Captain of Southampton (matches), Japan, Japan Olympic team, and LA Galaxy; vice-captain at Schalke
LA Galaxy Defender of the Year (a club award)
University degree from Waseda while playing in the Premier League (took about 12 years)
President of the Japan Pro-Footballers Association; started the player-voted JPFA Awards

leadership_intro: Short answer: he was almost never the most talented player in the room. He earned trust the slow way, and he did the same things again in every new country. Eight patterns show up again and again.

leadership.title: He planned for language years before he needed it
leadership.simple: He decided as a teenager that he wanted to play in Europe, then worked backward: 'So I must learn English now.' In each new country he learned the local language fast and used it in public, even when it was not perfect.
evidence: Chose a public high school partly so he could study English properly, already aiming abroad.
https://www.soccer-king.jp/sk_column/article/84825.html
Took English conversation lessons before leaving Japan; giving interviews in English by 2011.
https://gendai.media/articles/-/22834
Japan captain Hasebe handed him the job of talking to referees in English when he took over the armband (2017).
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/828172
Italy: used Genoa's local dialect in his debut-day interview, and it went viral. Six months later he did a club interview in Italian.
https://telenord.it/sampdoria-il-genovese-di-yoshida-e-virale-sul-web-cianin-cianin

leadership.title: He speaks up early instead of staying quiet
leadership.simple: Many foreign players stay silent until they feel safe. He does the opposite. He says what the team needs to hear, even as the new person.
evidence: Italy, 4 months in: shouted 'Parlate!' (Talk!) at a silent defence.
https://www.clubdoria46.it/sampdoria-parlate-urla-yoshida-la-difesa-e-muta/
Germany, 3 weeks in: said on TV that Schalke's squad was too big and had to improve.
https://www.watson.de/sport/fussball/640887259-schalke-04-maya-yoshida-mit-deutlichen-worten-zu-schalke-04-und-klassenerhalt
After the 2018 World Cup loss to Belgium he said Japan had been naive and fragile, and asked for a rethink of youth development.
https://inside.fifa.com/news/yoshida-japan-must-think-seriously-about-the-future
2021: publicly asked for the no-spectator decision at the Tokyo Olympics to be reconsidered.
https://www.footballchannel.jp/2021/07/18/post429576/

leadership.title: He takes the blame first, then explains
leadership.simple: When things go wrong he names his own mistake before anything else. This is a big reason people keep trusting him after bad days.
evidence: 2019 Asian Cup final: blamed himself for not removing the team's complacency.
https://www.soccer-king.jp/news/japan/national/20190204/902335.html
Schalke 2022: said his own performance was not good enough; he won his place back and the coach publicly asked for a new contract for him by March 2023.
https://www.goal.com/jp/%E3%83%8B%E3%83%A5%E3%83%BC%E3%82%B9/Bundesliga-Schalke-Maya-Yoshida-20230303/blt2161e75a2e5216e4
In 2024 he still said the Schalke relegation was his responsibility as a captain figure.
https://sportiva.shueisha.co.jp/clm/football/wfootball/2024/07/09/post_84/
2015: admitted his back-pass error against Manchester United to reporters straight after.
https://sportiva.shueisha.co.jp/clm/football/wfootball/2015/09/23/post_852/

leadership.title: He waits on the bench without complaining, then takes his chance
leadership.simple: At Southampton he was back-up for years under several managers. He did not complain in public. He fixed his weak points and was ready when the chance came.
evidence: Third-choice for long spells, then captain within months in 2017. Teammate Shinji Okazaki credited his patience.
https://news.livedoor.com/article/detail/12586536/
Manager Ronald Koeman praised his attitude and said he puts the team before himself (2015).
https://www.skysports.com/football/news/11700/9629102/southampton-defender-maya-yoshida-signs-a-new-three-year-contract
A review of his book notes he rarely criticises the managers who dropped him.
https://wsc.co.uk/?p=8248
LA Galaxy: said he first had to play well to earn trust; then started every league match of the 2024 title season at age 36.
https://www.lagalaxy.com/news/la-galaxy-announce-2024-team-awards

leadership.title: Humour and 'younger-brother power' make him easy to approach
leadership.simple: He is the youngest of three brothers and grew up in a house full of guests. He learned to get along with older people and to make people laugh. He calls this 'younger-brother power' (弟力).
evidence: Former J.League chairman Mitsuru Murai says Yoshida names 'younger-brother power' as his greatest strength.
https://president.jp/articles/-/64502?page=2
After his first Premier League match as captain he joked that the best part was not stumbling over the team talk.
https://www.footballchannel.jp/?p=206051
VVV-Venlo chairman Hai Berden remembers a cheerful, serious and responsible newcomer.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/813744

leadership.title: He gives back to the town he lives in
leadership.simple: He treats each city as home, not as a stop. Local people notice this, and it builds trust outside the dressing room too.
evidence: Southampton 2019: pledged 1% of his wages to the club's charity, to thank the city and set an example for young players.
https://www.premierleague.com/news/1312017
Genoa 2020: bought 10,000 masks for hospitals and club staff after playing only one match there.
https://www.sampdoria.it/en/news-en-2/team-en-2/2020/05/29/yoshida-donates-10000-protective-masks-to-genoa-hospitals-and-samp-employees/
Nagasaki: posts every 9 August (atomic bomb anniversary), in Japanese and English.
https://www.soccerdigestweb.com/news/detail/id=114846

leadership.title: He holds the door open for the next players
leadership.simple: He helps younger players, even the ones competing for his own position, and he guides Japanese players who move abroad after him.
evidence: Coached young defender Jack Stephens through his early matches; Stephens later named him the ex-teammate he would most want back.
https://sportsbeatfeed.co.uk/?p=11531
Takumi Minamino phoned him for advice before joining Southampton on loan (2021).
https://www.southamptonfc.com/en/news/article/minamino-reveals-yoshidas-influence
Yukinari Sugawara called him a legend; Yoshida texted him about the move and joked he could live in his house (2024).
https://www.southamptonfc.com/en/news/article/sugawara-inspired-by-legend-yoshida
Ran casual English lessons for younger Japan teammates at team meals.
https://president.jp/articles/-/64502

leadership.title: He leads even when he is not playing, and he builds systems
leadership.simple: Late in his career he showed that leadership is not only wearing the armband. He served the team from outside the squad, and he changed rules for all players through the union.
evidence: 2026 World Cup: gave up a TV job to travel as a non-playing support member, linking players and coaches.
https://www.lagalaxy.com/news/maya-yoshida-finds-a-new-way-to-lead-through-2026-world-cup-experience
Coach Hajime Moriyasu thanked him for unifying the players and for constant communication over the years.
https://www.soccer-king.jp/news/japan/national/20260530/2165095.html
Union president: J.League minimum salaries and the end of the old A/B/C contract system (decided 2024, from 2026).
https://daily.co.jp/soccer/2024/09/24/0018156230.shtml
Created the player-voted JPFA Awards (first ceremony Jan 2023), modelled on England's PFA awards.
https://www.soccer-king.jp/news/japan/japan_other/20230118/1730848.html

honest_view: He was not a flawless player. Famous mistakes: the 2015 back-pass against Manchester United, the handball in the 2019 Asian Cup final, and a saved penalty against Croatia in 2022.
Schalke was a failure on the pitch: the team was relegated and German media criticised him strongly.
He has only two major trophies (Asian Cup 2011 and MLS Cup 2024). His reputation is built on long service and leadership more than on winning.

'No other centre-back played in so many countries' is hard to prove. The safe statement: he played in the top division of six countries, which is very rare for any defender. I did not check every other player to prove he is the only one.
The claim that he was the 'first Japanese captain in the Premier League' is likely true but I could not find a source that proves it as a first.

roots.title: A house full of people
roots.text: His father liked a lively home and later opened a boarding house. Guests were always around, so Maya grew up talking with older people. He connects his easy way with people to this.

roots.title: Youngest of three brothers
roots.text: His eldest brother Honami, about seven years older and a goalkeeper, trained him hard and taught him to keep his head up. He practised on the steep slope outside the house.

roots.title: First club: Nanryo FC (南陵FC)
roots.text: He began at a local primary-school team in Nagasaki. He was a striker then. He started watching videos of his own matches at home as a child.

roots.title: Left home at 12
roots.text: He took the Nagoya Grampus youth trial 'as a souvenir' on a family trip and passed. A brother moved to Aichi to live with him. He was homesick, and seeing how much the move cost his family made him decide he had to become a professional.

roots.title: School and study
roots.text: He picked a public high school over the club-linked one so he would not get special treatment and could study English. He often studied through the night in exam periods. Later he finished a Waseda University degree by correspondence in 2019.

roots.title: From striker to centre-back
roots.text: His position moved backward as he grew: striker, then midfielder, then centre-back as a professional. Early mentors included Nagoya's Yutaka Akita, youth coach Park Jae-hyun, and first-team coaches Sef Vergoossen and Dragan Stojković.

roots.title: Nagasaki and peace
roots.text: He wrote a poem about war in second grade. As an adult he posts every 9 August about the atomic bombing, in two languages, and trains with hometown club V-Varen Nagasaki in the off-season.

roots.title: A promise to his father
roots.text: His father told his sons to dream big and not become 'football fools'. Number magazine reported that the 2024 MLS title fulfilled a promise to his late father.

personal.event: Announced his marriage on his blog (26 Sep UK time, 27 Sep in Japan). He wrote that they had been together four years, since his Nagoya Grampus days. His wife is a private person; her name is not public.
Announced on his blog that his first child, a daughter, was born at the end of November 2016 (exact day not public).
Scored his first goal as a father (FA Cup, against Norwich) and celebrated with a baby's-dummy gesture for his daughter.
Book 'Unbeatable Mind' published in English (HarperCollins); Japanese title レジリエンス――負けない力.
UK permanent residency reported; he said the test was the scariest he had taken.
Became president of the Japan Pro-Footballers Association.
Hosts a radio show on TOKYO FM (吉田麻也のチャレンジ&カバー).

Announced on Instagram that his second child, a son, had been born. He wrote that the last three months had been very busy, so the birth was probably around August 2025 (my reading; exact date not public).
Received a US green card (permanent residency).
Reported to hold a UEFA B coaching licence and to be working toward the A licence.
Said he is still in talks about his future, that passion for a project matters more than money, and that he believes he can still play once his knee heals.

No reliable report was found of a company he owns, an investment, or a football school.
No trustworthy source publishes his total career earnings or net worth. Websites that do are guessing.
'Guaranteed compensation' in MLS means base salary plus guaranteed bonuses, averaged per year. It is not exactly the cash paid in that year.
The 2023 to 2025 MLS numbers were seen through Spotrac and news reports, not read from the union's own files. The 2026 number was read directly.
money.changes_intro: A salary cap is a league rule that limits how much a team may pay all its players together. Major League Soccer (MLS) has a strict one: only three star players per team ('designated players') can be paid freely. Everyone else has to fit under the limit. That rule explains the biggest drop below.

changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: New three-year Southampton contract in August 2017, right after his breakthrough season: first matches as captain, a cup final, and 100 Premier League matches.

changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: His Southampton contract ended in June 2020 and he stayed at Sampdoria as a free agent on a one-year deal, reportedly with a pay cut. He was 31, and it was the first pandemic summer.

changes.label: ESTIMATE
changes.why: A one-year contract at Schalke, a club just promoted to the top division, at age 33.

changes.label: OFFICIAL (MLS figure)
changes.why: Joined LA Galaxy as a free agent after Schalke were relegated. He was not one of the team's three 'designated' stars, so his pay had to fit under the cap. He said he chose LA because the project excited him most.

changes.label: OFFICIAL
changes.why: Same contract. It was signed in August 2023 and ran through 2024. (In 2023 he was paid only for the part of the year he was there.)

changes.label: OFFICIAL
changes.why: The salary cap. His contract ended just as he won the title, so he had to sign a new one at the worst moment. The Galaxy needed to find over $1 million of space because two young players (Dejan Joveljić and Gabriel Pec) grew out of special low-cost youth contracts. The club traded away four players, including the final's best player, and still had to pay Yoshida less. The general manager called it 'a math problem, not a soccer problem.' Of the 14 players used in the final, he was the only one who had to renegotiate.

changes.label: His own words (LA Times)
changes.why: He called the cut unfair and said a champion should not be paid less. He had offers elsewhere and could have earned more. He stayed because the Galaxy offered two years, which let his daughter stay at one school, and kept him in the USA through the 2026 World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. He added that he needed to earn money outside football.

changes.label: OFFICIAL figure; reason NOT confirmed
changes.why: No report explains the rise. It was the second year of the same two-year contract, so the most likely reason is a raise written into the contract for year two (my reading, not confirmed). It was not the green card: the figures are dated April 2026 and the green card came in July.

changes.label: OFFICIAL
changes.why: Free agent. On 10 Nov 2026 he said passion for a project matters more to him than money.

unverified: Catholic faith and a rosary from the Vatican: found only on English Wikipedia. Not treated as fact here.
'I feel 25 percent English': the Japanese report of that interview has him joking that he understands about 25% of English. Exact wording unconfirmed.
Baseball pitcher Tsuyoshi Shimoyanagi as his 'uncle': Japanese Wikipedia describes a more distant relative.
Who the boarding house is for: one report says high-school students from remote islands; not confirmed directly.
Meaning of the name 'Maya': three different versions exist; he says his parents tell it differently each time.
Eredivisie Goal of the Season 2011–12: only English Wikipedia states the award.
Details of his 2010 foot injury differ between sources (all agree on about 10 months out).
'First Japanese to captain a Premier League team': likely, but no source proves it as a first.
2026 match count: Soccer King says 28 (used here); Rotowire says 23 league matches; Wikipedia is out of date.
LA Galaxy say '722 career appearances'; my season-by-season club total is 580 plus 127 Japan caps. The club may count differently.
All-time Japan caps rank (3rd): reported by Soccer King; the full list was not checked line by line.
Whether he is still union president after mid-2026: last confirmed in November 2025.
GM Will Kuntz's 20 Nov 2026 comments were read through Japanese reports, so wording is a translation.
Rumours linking him with V-Varen Nagasaki or Nagoya are fan talk and one tabloid report. Nothing official.
Direct YouTube links were not confirmed; the appendix uses YouTube search links by exact title.
A YouTube channel exists under his name, but I could not confirm it is official, so it is not linked.
Vera&John: I found no public comment from Yoshida himself, only his office's statement. The office statement was read through reports quoting Daily Shincho.
FIFA agent fee limits: introduced in 2023 and challenged in courts; current status not checked.
His agent in 2026: a 2021 article lists him with CAA Base; nothing newer was found. 'Introduced by Honda' rests on English Wikipedia and one fan-site article.
'Shootribe' appears as a management-company link on his Japanese Wikipedia page; what it is and who runs it is not confirmed.
Whether Kiyooka handled his 2012 move to Southampton is not confirmed.
Why his MLS pay rose from 2025 to 2026: no source found. A built-in raise for the second contract year is my reading, not a reported fact.
Who at LA Galaxy first contacted him in 2023, and what they told him: not found (only the first part of his interview on the move could be read).

The exact wording of the 2023 signing ban: one source says the club could not sign international players that summer; the league's website says it was in effect limited to free agents and trades within the league.
LA Galaxy finishing 11th in the West in 2026 comes from a fan-site summary, not an official table.
The ages of MLS signings come from one independent analysis; the league has not published its own figure here.
Full text of his old blog posts (Ameba, LINE BLOG): both blogs are offline; only news reports and short excerpts were read. Checked 21 Nov 2026.

videos.intro: I could not confirm direct YouTube links from my tools, so the YouTube rows are SEARCH links: click and the video with that exact title should be at or near the top. The other rows are direct links to official pages.

controversies.intro: No real scandal was found: no report of a crime, doping, match-fixing or a personal-life scandal in Japanese or English news (searched 21 Nov 2026). A search cannot prove nothing exists, so this section lists everything that did come up, big or small. Each row says what his part was.

items.title: Advertising for Vera&John 'free version' (an online casino brand)
items.what: He was the ambassador and appeared in its TV ads. In 2025, when Japanese comedians were questioned by police over online casino gambling, some people online said he, Shinji Okazaki and DAZN should be blamed, because free versions can lead people to the illegal real-money sites.
items.outcome: The free version takes no real-money bets and is treated as a 'game' in Japan, so the ad was not illegal. In Feb 2025 his management office said its understanding at the time was not enough and apologised. No action against him. See the deep dive below.

items.title: Asked for fans to be allowed at the Tokyo Olympics
items.what: During the pandemic he publicly asked for the no-spectator decision to be reconsidered. Public opinion in Japan was split at the time.
items.outcome: A public stance, not a scandal. Most Olympic venues stayed without spectators.

items.title: Confrontation with fans in Saudi Arabia
items.what: After a 1–0 loss he pointed angrily at the stands and said fans had made a discriminatory gesture. In 2026 he said he had been angry enough to try to throw the microphone, and only its wind cover came off.
items.outcome: Saudi fans and a former Saudi international apologised; the Japan FA said the Saudi federation apologised and punished the fans. The players' world union FIFPRO later used his case in an anti-racism campaign.

items.title: AFC social media post with a monkey emoji
items.what: Asia's football body posted a clip of his missed shot with a monkey emoji. Fans called it racist.
items.outcome: The AFC removed the emoji and changed the caption.

items.title: Online abuse and Wikipedia vandalism
items.what: His Wikipedia page was vandalised during a loss to Tunisia (he gave away a penalty) and again after the World Cup loss to Costa Rica.
items.outcome: The page was protected. As union president he later spoke out against online abuse of players.

items.title: Red cards, mistakes and the Schalke relegation
items.what: Sent off at the 2011 Asian Cup, in the Netherlands in 2012 and against Everton in 2018. Famous errors in 2015, 2019 and 2022. Strong criticism from German media at Schalke.
items.outcome: Normal football criticism. He answered it by taking the blame in public (see the leadership section).

deep_dives.title: The Vera&John ad deal: how a sports sponsorship really works
deep_dives.intro: Short version: Yoshida was the face, but four kinds of companies were involved besides him: the casino brand, an ad agency, his management office and the media. Each treated it the same way: 'it is only the free version, so it is legal.' That was true at the time. It still hurt his reputation four years later. No report says he gambled or broke any law.

cells: 1. The brand
Vera&John, an online casino licensed in Curaçao (a Caribbean island)
Its real-money casino is illegal to use from Japan. A police survey found it was the most-used online casino among Japanese users. It also ran a separate 'free version' site with no real money.
2. The ad agency
A+E Networks Japan (the company behind the History Channel in Japan)
Won the 'free version' account. Bought the ad space, made the commercial, did the PR, and announced the ambassador contract.
3. The athlete's office
Universal Music LLC (his management office in Japan for ads and media)
Received the offer and said yes on his behalf. In 2025 it said: 'our company accepted the request.'
4. The athlete
Maya Yoshida
Filmed the commercial in Italy in May 2021, became 'ambassador', hosted a sponsored podcast from April 2022, filmed a second commercial in 2023.
5. The media
DAZN, TV Asahi network, BS TV Tokyo, BS-TBS, AbemaTV, Spotify
Checked the ad against their own rules, passed it because it was a free game, and aired it.
May 2021
Commercial filmed in Italy while he played for Sampdoria. Japanese crew directed remotely because of COVID.
Ambassador contract announced. Ads start on DAZN, then on TV nationwide.
Sponsored Spotify podcast starts: 吉田麻也のオフサイドトーク! Supported by ベラジョン無料版.
June 2023
Contract ends (according to his office). In the same month the Japanese government publicly warned that using even a legally-run overseas casino from Japan can be a crime.
Feb 2025
Comedians and baseball players are investigated for online casino gambling. Some say they thought it was legal because they saw ads. Old pictures of Yoshida's commercial spread online.
Weekly magazine site Daily Shincho asks whether Yoshida is 'OK' as the face of the ads. An unnamed ad-agency source says celebrities were blinded by quick money.

His office answers Daily Shincho: it saw the job as a free online game with no cash; the contract covered only the free service and is not a gambling crime; but its understanding at the time 'was not enough'. It apologises to Yoshida and others for the trouble.
Mar 2025
Asahi Shimbun reports the legal blind spot for 'free version' ads. DAZN says it allowed them because they were free games. Vera&John says it no longer runs the ads.
Japan changes the law: advertising or guiding people to online casinos is now banned. First arrests of casino-ad website operators follow.

parts.heading: What we can learn about the sports business (my analysis)
rows: 'Legal' and 'safe for your name' are different things. Everyone in the chain checked the law. Nobody's job was to ask 'how will this look in five years?'
The athlete is the only face. Several companies earned money, but the public remembers one person. The risk and the reward are not shared equally.
An athlete has two kinds of helpers. The agent handles clubs and contracts. A separate management office handles ads and TV. The ad deal came through the second one, not through his football agent.
Timing matters. The deal was made during COVID, when sport lost income and gambling brands had large ad budgets. That is context, not an excuse.
https://www.sportmediarights.tokyo/posts/56427674
Rules change later. In 2021 these ads passed every TV station's checks. From September 2025 the same kind of promotion is banned. Old deals get judged by new standards.
The office took the blame in public. Its statement says the company accepted the job and apologises to him. I found no public comment from Yoshida himself.
https://www.dailyshincho.jp/article/2025/02280605/?all=1&page=3
It connects to his union work. As players' union president he has pushed for players to control their own image rights. This case shows why who decides how a player's face is used matters.
https://www.soccer-king.jp/news/japan/20251117/2088713.html

deep_dives.title: When he was a target, and how he came through it
deep_dives.intro: A sports magazine wrote in 2022 that he may be the most criticised player in Japan national team history. A centre-back's mistakes become goals, so he was blamed often. The pattern in how he answered is the same each time.

cells: June 2013

Confederations Cup vs Italy: his mistake led to a goal. Media and fans treated him as the one to blame, and coach Zaccheroni said he was not at international level. He admitted it hurt, joking that in his next life he would be a forward.
Kept his place over time; four years later he became the first Japanese player to reach 100 Premier League matches.
After the World Cup a tabloid named him among those to blame for Japan's failure; he was also a reserve at Southampton.
Stayed, fought for his place, signed a new contract in January 2015.
Feb 2019
Asian Cup final: his handball gave Qatar a penalty.
Blamed himself in public for the team's complacency and changed how he led.
Oct 2021
Saudi fans made a discriminatory gesture during his interview.
Confronted it on the spot, named it as discrimination to the media. Apologies followed, and the players' world union used his story in an anti-racism campaign.
Mar 2022
Japan under heavy criticism in World Cup qualifying.
Said the team 'planted the seeds' itself, that the national team is where you take the arrows, and told younger players to turn criticism into energy. Japan qualified the next day.
Nov 2022
World Cup: his pass led to Costa Rica's winning goal. Harsh abuse online; his Wikipedia page was vandalised.
Four days later he captained Japan to a win over Spain.
Aug 2024
Rising online abuse and privacy attacks on players.
As union president he issued a public statement asking media and social networks to respect players' and families' privacy.

parts.heading: His method, in five steps (my reading of the pattern)
rows: 1. Say it first. He names his own mistake before critics do.
2. Do not feed on it. He says to focus on the job, not on 'sticky' online criticism.
https://www.tokyo-sports.co.jp/articles/-/165015
3. Answer in the next match. The reply to Costa Rica was Spain.
4. Draw a line at discrimination. Criticism of his play he accepts; racism he confronts in public.
5. Turn it into rules. He used the union to speak for all players, so the next player has more protection than he had.

deep_dives.title: Sports agents and Japanese players abroad
deep_dives.intro: An agent is the person who finds clubs and negotiates contracts for a player. For a Japanese player, the agent is also the bridge to a football market on the other side of the world. Yoshida says he tells younger players there are two choices they must never get wrong: their wife and their agent. For the full picture, see the Agents section of this database (overview, Tetsuro Kiyooka, Thomas Kroth).

cells: The introduction
Keisuke Honda, his teammate at Nagoya, introduced him to his agent, Tetsuro Kiyooka (per English Wikipedia).
The agent
Kiyooka passed the Japan FA agent exam around 2006 and was Honda's agent at his 2008 signing for VVV-Venlo. One article credits him with arranging Yoshida's move there.
The gateway club

Both Honda and Yoshida went first to VVV-Venlo, a small Dutch club. The door was opened by its chairman, Hai Berden, who did business with Japan, and by Sef Vergoossen, a Dutch coach who had worked at Nagoya. The agent represented the player at the table.
The step up
From VVV he moved to Southampton in 2012 for about £3 million, later called one of the club's best pieces of business.
Agent and union

Kiyooka was also an executive of the Japanese players' association from about 2009. In December 2010 he was its spokesman in a pay and image-rights fight with the Japan FA, and a boycott was hinted. The association became a labour union in 2011.
Later
Yoshida became president of that same union in 2022 and in 2025 pushed again for players' image rights. No source shows Kiyooka and Yoshida working on union matters together.
Today

A 2021 Number article lists Yoshida as a client of CAA Base, a London agency that charges Japanese players no fee. Whether that still holds in 2026 is not confirmed. Kiyooka is now described as a former agent.

parts.heading: How the agent business works for Japanese players

cells: Who pays the agent?
In Japan, usually the player: about 5–10% of salary. In Germany, by custom the club pays. A newer model (the agency CAA Base) charges the player nothing and is paid by clubs.
Why a local partner matters
A German agent, Thomas Kroth, handled almost every Japanese move to Germany's Bundesliga from 2002. He said selling directly from Japan is hard: Asia is far, and clubs look at nearby countries first.
Japanese pioneers
Nobuaki Tanabe got his FIFA licence in 1999, when Japan had only about 10 agents, and took Junichi Inamoto to Arsenal in 2001.
The real work
Tanabe says negotiating is only one or two days a year. The rest is helping the player improve, for example with match video and data.
The rules keep changing

Until 2015: FIFA licence. 2015–2023: no licence, anyone could register as an 'intermediary'. Since October 2023: FIFA licence and exam again, with about 4,500 licences worldwide. A Japanese report puts the exam pass rate near 8%.
Fee limits
FIFA's 2023 rules set a limit of 3% on bigger deals and 5% on smaller ones. These limits have been challenged in courts; I did not confirm their status today.

rows: A club usually contacts the agent first, saying which position it needs. The agent offers names.

https://qoly.jp/q1/17857240

https://qoly.jp/q1/17857240/p2

https://qoly.jp/q1/17857240/p2

https://qoly.jp/q1/17857240/p2
His advice to younger players: choosing a wife and choosing an agent are the two decisions you cannot get wrong, because a footballer's career is short.
https://qoly.jp/q1/17813172

deep_dives.title: LA Galaxy and MLS: who owns the club, how it grew, and why he could join
deep_dives.intro: Short version: he joined because the club was in trouble. In summer 2023 the Galaxy were near the bottom, banned from buying players from abroad, and missing an injured centre-back. A new recruitment chief needed an experienced leader who cost no transfer fee. Yoshida was a free agent who wanted a decision before August and a good place for his family.

cells: The owner
AEG (Anschutz Entertainment Group), a sports and concert company. It also owns the LA Kings ice hockey team and big arenas.
The person behind it

Philip Anschutz, a billionaire from Denver who made his money in oil, railroads and telecoms. He became interested in soccer during the 1994 World Cup and was a co-founder and lead investor of Major League Soccer (MLS).
Since when
AEG bought the Galaxy in October 1998. In the league's early years AEG ran six MLS clubs at once to keep the league alive. Today it runs only the Galaxy.
Who runs it day to day
AEG's chief executive Dan Beckerman oversees it. Will Kuntz has been general manager since December 2023, and Greg Vanney head coach since January 2021.
How MLS ownership is different

MLS is a 'single entity': the league itself holds the player contracts, and each club has an 'investor-operator' who is a shareholder in the league. That is why the league can set one salary limit for everyone.
One of the ten original MLS clubs. Plays at the huge Rose Bowl and reaches the first final.
Moves into its own 27,000-seat soccer stadium, paid for by the owner. Becomes the first MLS team to make a profit.
Signs David Beckham from Real Madrid. MLS creates the 'designated player' rule so a club can pay a few stars outside the salary limit. The Galaxy become the league's glamour club.
Three titles in four years with Beckham, Landon Donovan and Robbie Keane. Five titles in total, a league record.
More famous names (Steven Gerrard, Zlatan Ibrahimović, Javier 'Chicharito' Hernández) but no titles. Last place in 2017. A new local rival, LAFC, arrives in 2018.
Dec 2022
MLS punishes the club for breaking salary rules on a 2019 signing: it loses $1 million of spending allowance, the president is suspended, and it may not sign players from abroad in summer 2023.
Early 2023
Worst start in club history. Supporters boycott home games to demand the president's removal. He leaves on 30 May.
April 2023
Will Kuntz arrives from rival LAFC to run recruitment.
Aug 2023
Yoshida signs.
Sixth title, first in ten years, with Yoshida as captain.
The salary limit breaks up the champions; star midfielder Riqui Puig is injured for two seasons; 14th and then 11th in the West.

parts.heading: Why he was able to join in 2023
rows: The club could not buy. Because of the punishment, it was limited that summer to free agents and trades inside the league.
https://www.mlssoccer.com/news/la-galaxy-how-one-of-mls-s-most-storied-clubs-got-their-swagger-back
It had a hole in defence. Starting centre-back Martín Cáceres had a season-ending knee injury, and the team had won only three of its first 19 league matches.
https://www.mlssoccer.com/news/la-galaxy-how-one-of-mls-s-most-storied-clubs-got-their-swagger-back
He was free. Schalke's relegation ended his contract, so no transfer fee was needed. The league's own website describes him as available as a free agent after Schalke went down.
https://www.mlssoccer.com/news/la-galaxy-how-one-of-mls-s-most-storied-clubs-got-their-swagger-back
A new recruiter wanted leaders. Kuntz's first signings were Yoshida and other experienced players for the club's most urgent needs.
https://laxsportsnation.com/2023/12/08/the-la-galaxy-finally-have-a-general-manager/
He did not need a star's contract. He was not one of the three 'designated players', so his $800,000 fitted under the salary limit.
https://www.spotrac.com/mls/player/_/id/85703/maya-yoshida

His own reasons. At 35 he expected European offers to come only late in August and did not want to wait. He thought about the Middle East but worried about his family. When the Galaxy's offer came he thought 'this is it'.
https://sportiva.shueisha.co.jp/clm/football/wfootball/2024/07/08/post_83/
The Japanese link came after him, not before. Japan defender Miki Yamane joined in 2024, and forward Kyogo Furuhashi followed later.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LA_Galaxy

parts.heading: How MLS brings in players from overseas

cells: Designated players (since 2007)
Up to three stars per club can be paid outside the salary limit. These are the famous names.
David Beckham; Lionel Messi (2023); Son Heung-min (2025, a league-record fee of about $26 million)
Young talent (U22 Initiative, since 2021)
Up to three young players per club count cheaply against the limit. Clubs buy them young, often from South America, and hope to sell them to Europe later.
Dejan Joveljić and Gabriel Pec at the Galaxy
Experienced free agents
Players whose contracts ended in Europe. No transfer fee, modest pay, valued for leadership.
Maya Yoshida (2023)
Everyone else
Must fit under the salary limit, sometimes helped by extra spending allowances the league hands out.
Most of each squad

parts.heading: Is it a league for players near retirement?
rows: Partly, for the famous ones. Messi, Luis Suárez, Thomas Müller and Robert Lewandowski were all over 34 when they signed. Son was 33.
https://coverthepitch.substack.com/p/is-major-league-soccer-really-a-retirement
Not for the typical signing. One analysis of the summer 2026 window found the average age of players coming from abroad was 26 years and 8 months, about the same as the two years before.
https://coverthepitch.substack.com/p/is-major-league-soccer-really-a-retirement
Spending is rising. MLS clubs spent a record $336 million on players in one 2025 window.
https://www.goal.com/en-us/lists/mls-shatters-spending-record-with-usd336-million-transfer-window-fueled-by-deals-sending-son-heung-min-to-lafc-and-rodrigo-de-paul-to-inter-miami/blt8f859428c1b690e6

So there are two leagues in one: a few older stars who sell tickets and shirts, and many players in their mid-20s. The old stars get the headlines, which is why it looks like a retirement league from far away. (My reading of the numbers.)
Yoshida's own criticism: the salary limit means players who are not stars earn relatively little, and he said the league needs to grow financially if it wants good players to come.
https://www.aol.com/news/galaxy-captain-maya-yoshida-gets-120020178.html

parts.heading: What we can learn (my analysis)
rows: A club's bad moment can be a player's opening. He was signed because the Galaxy were restricted, injured and losing.
Being a free agent is a strength at the right time. A club that cannot pay a transfer fee can still sign you.
The same rule that let him in later cut his pay. The salary limit made room for a $800,000 leader in 2023 and squeezed him to $455,000 in 2025.
Owners shape careers from far away. One investor kept the league alive in its early years, built the stadium, and his company still decides who runs the club.

deep_dives.title: His old blogs (2012–2016): what they add
deep_dives.intro: He wrote two official blogs: one on Ameba (to about 2015) and one on LINE BLOG (from 2016). Both are gone. The Ameba address returned 'page not found' on 21 Nov 2026, and the LINE BLOG service has closed. Saved copies exist on the Internet Archive, but my tools cannot open that site, so this table uses news reports from the time and a bookmark site that kept short excerpts. Summaries are in my own words. The last column is my reading.

cells: London Olympics: his first goal of the tournament
He dedicates the goal to his mother, whose birthday it was.
Family comes first in his public voice.
After the Olympic semi-final loss
Says he is more frustrated than he has been in a long time, will let himself feel it for one day, then move on to the bronze-medal match.
The same pattern as chapter 1: own the pain, then look forward.
Leaving VVV-Venlo for Southampton
Says his two and a half years in Venlo were mostly hard and he nearly gave up many times. He thanks his Dutch host family and the Japanese players living nearby.
Shows who carried him through the injury year: a local family and fellow Japanese players, not only the club.
Marriage announcement
Says he married that summer after four years together, and that he wants her support so he can focus on the Premier League. A sports paper's front page had leaked the news a few hours earlier.
He married right as he moved to England, and he told fans himself once the news was out.
First goal of the season, against Everton
Says sliding on his knees like Steven Gerrard after scoring in England had been a long-time dream.
His humour, and how much the Premier League meant to him.
70 years after the Nagasaki atomic bomb
Writes that first-hand voices are disappearing. He visited Nagasaki for a TV news programme and listened to survivors in person.
The root of the 9 August posts he still makes every year.
Life abroad
Writes about missing Japan, needing results to keep his place, and not being happy with his play at full-back even though he scored.
Honest self-criticism during his bench years at Southampton.
Birth of his daughter
Announces the birth (end of November) with a joke about a 'parent-and-child contract', and in the same post announces a support deal with Japan Airlines (JAL).
A sponsor deal I had not listed before. It is now in the money chapter.

parts.heading: Posts that still leave a trace
What else was on the blogs
rows: Regular topics in the surviving excerpts: jokes about teammates (Atsuto Uchida and Makoto Hasebe appear often), travel on days off, and thanks to fans.
https://b.hatena.ne.jp/site/ameblo.jp/mayayoshida/
Not found in what survives: anything about agents, contracts or money.

fan_voices.intro: These are opinions from ordinary readers, not facts. They show how fans feel, and they are sometimes wrong. Nothing in this section is used anywhere else in this profile. No usernames are kept and no comment is copied; each theme is described in my own words.

samples.source: Yahoo! News Japan comments on the Nikkan Sports article about him leaving LA Galaxy
samples.sample: The top 30 of 141 reader comments in 'recommended' order (179 including replies), plus 1 comment from a commentator labelled as an expert by Yahoo. Top comments are the most liked, so this is not a fair sample of all readers.
themes: The biggest theme. Readers want to see him finish in the J.League and pass on his experience. Clubs named: Nagasaki (3), Nagoya (2), Iwata (1).

He is called a legend. Readers list the countries he played in, the famous defenders he competed with at Southampton, and how rarely he was injured. One of the two most-liked comments praised 117 matches in three and a half years at his age.
Readers expect him to work one day for the Japan FA or Asia's football body, or to reform Japanese football.
Several say his English and the many European coaches he played under would make him a good manager, perhaps abroad.
He may stay in the USA
Readers point to his green card and his family. The single most-liked comment said he could find another US club or return to Japan.

Calls for him to join hometown club V-Varen Nagasaki drew more 'hmm' reactions than agreement in two of three cases. One well-received comment argued he left Nagasaki at 12 and has deeper ties to Aichi.
One reader wondered whether having no new club announced means no offers. No abusive comments appeared in the top 30.
notes: The expert-labelled comment said American reporters who cover the team rated him highly even as his playing time fell late in the season.
An example of why comments are not facts: one reader wrote that he got his green card 'last year'. The reported date is July 2026.
Yahoo also shows an AI summary of the comments. It appeared masked in the page text, so it was not used.

own_words.intro: Posts from his own account. These are his statements, so they count as first-hand. A claim about facts (a transfer, a fee, an injury) still needs a news report or official page before it goes into the timeline.
own_words.note: Read without a login, so some posts may be missing. As of this date there was no post about leaving LA Galaxy or his next step.
